extracted.intended_audience: poets, authors, critics, and readers interested in aesthetics and taste
extracted.subtask_short: writing for the sublime and beautiful
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and evaluative criteria for producing and judging the sublime and the beautiful in language, visual art, and other imaginative arts; includes causes, sensations, and rhetorical techniques that produce aesthetic effects. Useful for creative writers and critics wanting to shape or assess powerful expressive effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of Taste / common principles
rubrics_metrics.description: There are principles on which the imagination is affected, 'so common to all, so grounded and certain, as to supply the means of reasoning satisfactorily about them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taste is not wholly caprice; basic standards exist because senses and imagination operate similarly across humans. Seek principles grounded in natural impressions and shared perception rather than eccentric personal whim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senses as the foundation of taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasures and pains deriving from the senses are substantially the same in all men; what appears light, sweet, or bitter to one will to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming for universal response, build on basic sensory impressions (light/dark, sweet/bitter, large/small, soft/hard). Use these as stable foundations for aesthetic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination: pleasure from resemblance
rubrics_metrics.description: The imagination is chiefly pleased by tracing resemblances; 'it has naturally a far greater alacrity and satisfaction in tracing resemblances than in searching for differences.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use apt metaphors, similitudes and striking resemblances to gratify the imagination; novelty of association pleases. Distinctions and critical refinements please less instantly and require knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty is treated as a distinct topic (Part I, Sect. I) influencing pleasure and attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce new or unexpected elements to catch attention, but balance novelty with recognisable resemblance so the imagination can respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pain and Pleasure (and their interplay)
rubrics_metrics.description: The nature and relation of pain and pleasure shape aesthetic responses (Part I, Sect. II & III).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explore contrasts: removal of pain vs positive pleasure, and how negative and positive affective states contribute differently to aesthetic delight or awe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delight versus Pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between delight and mere pleasure (Part I, Sect. IV).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for delight (a higher, complex pleasure often tied to imagination and moral/emotional engagement) rather than simple sensory pleasure when seeking deeper effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passions of Self-preservation and Society
rubrics_metrics.description: Different passions arise from self-preservation versus social relations and these map onto different aesthetic effects (Part I, Sect. VI—IX).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage which class of passion you intend to arouse: fear/terror and awe (self-preservation) versus pity, sympathy, admiration (social) — they operate by different mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Sublime (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: A central classificatory head: qualities and causes that produce the passion of the sublime are distinct from those producing the beautiful (Part I, Sect. VII; Part II).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sublime arises from greatness, power, obscurity, terror, vastness, infinity, difficulty, privation, succession, &c.; to produce sublime effects, foreground those properties rather than delicate, smooth, small features of beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terror as a source of the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: Terror (fear) is foundational to the passion caused by the sublime (Part II, Sect. II).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To generate the sublime, evoke a controlled sense of terror or danger — not mere shock, but a regulated awe-producing fear that engages imagination and sympathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscurity and its power
rubrics_metrics.description: Obscurity increases the sublime by withholding clear perception and thereby enlarging imagination (Part II, Sect. III—IV).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use obscurity, ambiguity, or vagueness deliberately (e.g., darkness, indistinctness) to provoke dread, wonder, and the mind's tendency to fill gaps with vast imaginations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power
rubrics_metrics.description: Power (of an object) is a cause of sublime feeling (Part II, Sect. V).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represent overwhelming power (natural or moral) to produce awe; emphasize agency, force, or capability beyond ordinary scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privation
rubrics_metrics.description: Privation (absence or loss) contributes to the sublime (Part II, Sect. VI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use absence, emptiness, or loss (e.g., barren landscapes, voids) to inspire a sublime sense of lack that the imagination amplifies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vastness and Infinity
rubrics_metrics.description: Vastness and ideas of infinity produce the sublime (Part II, Sect. VII—VIII, XI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invoke scale beyond comprehension — great distance, duration, or multiplicity — to overwhelm the mind and create sublime awe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Succession and Uniformity
rubrics_metrics.description: Succession and uniformity in phenomena influence sublime responses (Part II, Sect. IX).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repetition, vast sequences, or uniform expanses to suggest interminability and intensify sublimity (or break uniformity to create dramatic effect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude in Building / Architectural Sublimity
rubrics_metrics.description: Magnitude and certain treatments in architecture contribute to the sublime (Part II, Sect. X, XV).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In descriptive prose/setting, treat built scale, vaulting, and light in architectures as tools to give a sense of awe (high vaults, colossal forms, dramatic lighting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Light and Darkness
rubrics_metrics.description: Light and especially darkness (and obscurity of darkness) have distinct effects: darkness can be terrible 'in its own nature' (Part II, Sect. XIV—XVI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manipulate illumination (or the absence of it) to produce either consoling beauty (light) or terrifying sublimity (darkness, shadows, blackness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Colour as productive of the Sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: Colour can contribute to the sublime if used to suggest vastness, obscurity, or power (Part II, Sect. XVI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose colours and tonal schemes that support the intended effect: sombre, deep, or stark palettes for sublime; delicate, bright palettes for beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sound and Loudness
rubrics_metrics.description: Sound (especially loudness, suddenness, intermitting) affects the sublime (Part II, Sect. XVII—XIX).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In writing, use rhythm, cadence, and onomatopoeia to simulate loud or sudden sounds; employ abruptness and silence (intermitting) to heighten tension and awe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suddenness and Intermittence
rubrics_metrics.description: Sudden, intermittent phenomena contribute to the sublime by surprising the imagination (Part II, Sect. XVIII—XIX, XXI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surprise and irregularity — sudden events, intermittent occurrences — displace expectation and can generate awe or terror.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smell, Taste, and Feeling (pain)
rubrics_metrics.description: Smell and taste (bitters and stenches) and bodily feeling/pain can produce strong affective responses relevant to the sublime or ugly (Part II, Sect. XXI—XXII).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ evocative sensory detail (including unpleasant senses) to ground emotional reactions; physical discomfort can provoke strong sympathy and intensity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion is not the cause of Beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportion (mathematical or formal symmetry) is argued not to be the real cause of beauty in vegetables, animals, or humans (Part III, Sect. II—IV).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't assume perfect proportion alone produces beauty; focus instead on qualitative features (smoothness, delicacy, variation) and perceived fitness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fitness is not the cause of Beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Fitness (usefulness or appropriate function) is not the true cause of beauty though it has real effects (Part III, Sect. VI—VII).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While appropriateness can enhance appreciation, beauty often depends on sensory qualities independent of utilitarian fitness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfection is not the cause of Beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfection (technical or mechanical excellence) is not identical with beauty (Part III, Sect. IX).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for qualities that please the imagination (smoothness, delicacy, gradation) rather than mere technical flawlessness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smoothness, Gradual Variation, and Delicacy (real causes of beauty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Smoothness, gradual variation, and delicacy are presented as real causes of beauty (Part III, Sect. XIV—XVI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For beautiful effects emphasise polished textures, gentle transitions, subtle detail, and refinement rather than stark contrasts or roughness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty in Colour, Sound, and Feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Colour, sound, and internal feelings can be beautiful; these modes each have their specific qualities that produce beauty (Part III, Sect. XVII, XXIV, XXV).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor colour imagery, musical cadence, and description of feeling to cultivate beauty: harmony, mellowness, and pleasing proportion of sensory elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Sublime and Beautiful compared
rubrics_metrics.description: The sublime and the beautiful are distinct sets of qualities and often opposed; the text repeatedly compares their differing causes and effects (Part III, Sect. XXVII).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether a passage aims for sublime (awe, terror, vastness) or beautiful (tenderness, smoothness, harmony) and avoid mixing cues that undermine the intended effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficient Cause and Association
rubrics_metrics.description: Association (experience and learned connections) and the efficient causes of passions (Part IV, Sect. I—II) mediate how objects produce sublime/beautiful feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use associative context, analogy, and cultural references carefully: past experience and learned associations can amplify or alter aesthetic responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Why large visual dimensions are sublime; unity for vastness
rubrics_metrics.description: Large visual dimensions provoke sublimity; unity is requisite to the perception of vastness (Part IV, Sect. IX—X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating vast scenes, provide a unifying principle (repetition, alignment, horizon) so the mind recognizes scale rather than perceiving chaos.

rubrics_metrics.name: The artificial infinite / vibrations similar
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques producing the idea of infinity (artificial infinite) and similarity of vibrations (repetition) are mechanisms for the sublime (Part IV, Sect. XI—XII).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rhetorical or descriptive devices that suggest boundlessness (endless repetition, unresolved sequences) to create a sense of infinity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words can affect without raising images
rubrics_metrics.description: Words often affect by means other than producing vivid sensory images; 'poetry... may lose a very considerable part of its energy if this were the necessary result of all description.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on abstract, cumulative, or suggestive language to move readers: implication, cadence, and associative phrasing can be more powerful than literal pictorial detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry not strictly an imitative art
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry 'is not strictly an imitative art' beyond dramatizing manners and passions; descriptive poetry operates 'chiefly by substitution' using sounds and customary effects of words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't aim solely to reproduce reality; use language as substitution and representation—the emotional effect of words can replace literal depiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: How words influence the passions (three causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Words influence passions chiefly by (1) conveying the speaker's own passion so we sympathise, (2) representing affecting subjects that rarely occur in reality but are powerfully felt in language, and (3) enabling combinations and circumstances impossible in other arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing, (1) convey authentic affective tone to enlist reader sympathy; (2) describe extraordinary or archetypal events/larger-than-life situations that resonate; (3) combine circumstances and modifiers (additions) to magnify emotional force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear expression versus strong expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish 'clear expression' (serves understanding) from 'strong expression' (serves the passions); often the latter moves more than the former.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose between clarity and force according to goal: for intellectual exposition prefer clarity; for moving the reader aim for forceful, passionate diction—even at some cost to literal clearness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of aggregation/one-word annexation to magnify
rubrics_metrics.description: A single well-chosen word appended to a list can vastly amplify effect (example: '—of Death').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit cumulative lists and end-weighted modifiers to produce a culminating shock or expansion (build many particular items then add a single grandizing term).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sympathy, Imitation, and Ambition (social mechanisms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sympathy, imitation, and ambition operate to spread feelings and modulate taste (Part I, Sect. XII—XVII).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage social emotions: create characters, situations, or attitudes that readers can imitate or sympathise with to diffuse emotional impact beyond isolated description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of words: general words before ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: General words often function before detailed ideas; many poetic effects proceed without producing distinct images (Part V sections on words).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use general, elevated diction when you want to evoke grandeur or mythic scope rather than to paint precise particulars.
